Article Title: Stop, think, check: 5.7 lakhs kids learn to question answers
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For Paresh Das, a class 10 student of Srimaa Govt High School, the most important lesson was not how to answer faster, but when to slow down. "Earlier, I used to answer quickly. During this activity, I realised that I should think about my answer first," he said. His new four-step rule: "Stop, think, ask and check."That shift from instinctive response to reasoned judgement is at the heart of the AM/NS India Times Critical Thinking Championship (TCTC), which has reached 5,68,653 students across 3,562 schools in 959 cities and 26 states and Union territories.Significantly, the intervention is concentrated at an age when learning habits are still taking shape. Of all participants, 4.3 lakh - nearly three-fourths - are in classes 3 to 8. Class 3 alone accounts for 94,873 students, followed by class 6 with 71,436, class 7 with 70,000 and class 8 with 66,998. Another 90,536 students are in classes 9 and 10.UP accounts for the largest share, with 3,98,266 participants, followed by Uttarakhand at 82,138, Himachal Pradesh at 42,617 and Bihar at 41,112, with smaller cohorts spread across other states.The initiative uses interactive sessions and scenario-based questions to help students distinguish fact from opinion, identify assumptions, examine evidence and explain how they reached a conclusion.The focus is less on supplying the correct answer and more on making the reasoning behind it visible.That distinction is becoming more important in classrooms where two powerful forces coexist: an examination culture that has traditionally rewarded recall and a digital environment where search engines, social media and AI can produce answers almost instantly. Information is abundant; verification, reasoning and judgment are becoming the scarcer skills.Student responses show how that difference is being understood. "Normally I have to learn, remember. Here I have to think," said one student from Sreema Govt High School, adding that asking questions while learning could also help in remembering subjects better.Another student said the sessions offered a different way of handling problems: instead of panicking, ask why the problem arose, break it down and work through possible answers. "The solution then becomes obvious," the student said.A third response went directly to the challenge of navigating competing information. "Many times we get confused about what to believe from many versions, how to reach a conclusion," the student said, arguing that STOP-THINK-ASK-CHECK could become a useful habit for getting closer to the truth.This is also the direction in which NEP 2020 and the National Curriculum Framework 2023 seek to move school learning - away from rote reproduction towards competency, application and conceptual understanding. But policy can change question papers faster than it changes classroom habits. Critical thinking requires students to be rewarded not merely for knowing, but for questioning, testing and, when necessary, revising what they think they know.In the AI era, that may become education's harder test. Machines can increasingly generate the first answer. Students will need to know whether it deserves to be the final one.
Article Summary: The AM/NS India Times Critical Thinking Championship has reached 5,68,653 students across 3,562 schools in 959 cities and 26 states and Union territories. Of all participants, 4.3 lakh - nearly three-fourths - are in classes 3 to 8.

Article Title: Trump’s new H-1B visa reality for Indians: Unpredictable costs, tougher odds, greater risks
Article Text:
The H-1B visa route is becoming more selective, compliance-intensive, and less forgiving.

But, Indian professionals who are evaluating career prospects in the US must understand not only the immediate regulatory changes, but also the longer-term implications for career mobility, employer sponsorship and immigration planning. The H-1B visa route is becoming more selective, compliance-intensive, and less forgiving. Here’s what you should know:

H-1B visa changes : What you should know

H-1B Visa Changes: Timeline of Important Events

New H-1B wage-weighted lottery

So what does all of this mean for your H-1B prospects?

What about existing H-1B holders facing layoffs?

Top source countries for H-1B visas

USCIS archived the guidance that let terminated workers use B-2 for job search, and immigration attorneys are steering clients away from using B-2 as a bridge as a result. The May 2026 USCIS Adjustment of Status memo now treats in-country green card adjustment as extraordinary discretionary relief. Footnote 20 of the memo says holding H-1B status alone is not sufficient to justify adjustment.

H-1B: Ranking of Top Employers

Demand stays strong, but alternative destinations in focus

What Indian professionals should consider

H-1B Selection Rate By Wage Level

India EB-2 pending: about 351,000.

India EB-3 pending: about 105,000.

India EB-1 filings jumped from 12,006 in FY2024 to 14,248 in FY2025, and denials on those filings ran at 22% (vs. 9% in FY2024). Indians are pouring into EB-1 as EB-2 stalls, and USCIS is denying more of it.

Has the Donald Trump administration effectively killed the H-1B visa dream? Frequent policy changes, increasing restrictions and selective picking - the H-1B visa path for Indian professionals is becoming tougher to navigate - with unpredictability serving as the biggest obstruction.H-1B visas have long been the main road for Indian professionals who are seeking employment, long-term career opportunities, and eventually even the green card in the US. But over the past two years, several changes in the H-1B visa application and selection criterion have added a huge layer of uncertainty.Which is not to say that Indians still don’t make up the biggest chunk of individuals being granted the H-B visas. This is particularly true for engineering, technology, financial services, healthcare, and research-driven industries.Also Read | Indian IT sector job market is changing: What can get you hired & at a premium Higher H-1B application fee (under litigation as of now), a new selection process, new rules for the 60-day grace period - the process has seen several changes recently.Xiao Wang, CEO of Boundless Immigration points out the three things that have changed in the last year, and how they are compounding the uncertainty:First, the $100,000 fee. Boundless’ CEO is of the view that the fee has dissuaded external applications from India in the first cap season under it, and that India-based IT consulting firms have absorbed the biggest hit, since their model depends on sending people to the US from India.“The National Foundation for American Policy documented the shift on the employer side: the top four H-1B employers in FY2025 are Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Google, not the Indian IT firms that historically held those slots,” Xiao Wang tells TOI.The fee has recently been struck down by a US court, but is likely to be appealed by the Trump administration.Second, the wage-weighted lottery. USCIS ran the March 2026 cap season under new rules that favor higher-paid workers. “In our Boundless client data, Level III (senior) candidates were selected at 68%, and Level I (entry level) candidates at 40%. For Indian professionals coming out of US master's programs into their first job, that gap matters,” he says.Third, the sharp drop in EB-1A approvals. The USCIS I-140 report for Q2 FY2026 (Jan-Mar 2026) puts the EB-1A approval rate at 41.7%, down from 66.9% for FY2025 as a whole.In the same USCIS I-140 country data, Indian nationals filed 1,761 of the 6,647 EB-1A receipts worldwide in Q2 FY2026, 26.5% of the total.“Our read is that the drop in approvals lands disproportionately on Indian applicants because they are the single largest filer population in the category,” he says.According to K Edward Raleigh, Partner at Fragomen, a global immigration law firm, the new selection system gives greater weight to higher-paid and higher-skilled positions rather than relying on a purely random selection process.“That potentially creates advantages for some highly skilled professionals while making the process more challenging for others,” he tells TOI.Once you have received an H-1B visa, the road is somewhat smoother. Experts say renewing the H-1B is still a routine process.According to Boundless, the NFAP November 2025 report puts the continuing employment denial rate at 1.9% for FY2025, which is essentially unchanged from 1.8% in FY2024.But, there are risks associated with layoffs, which then initiates the 60-day grace period for visa holders to find an alternative job.“An H-1B worker who does not line up a new sponsoring employer or change status within 60 days falls out of status,” notes Xiao Wang, adding that two protections that used to make that window survivable are now weaker.There is also an added factor: The cost of keeping an existing H-1B worker could become more expensive. The Trump administration is considering extending the additional $4,000 H-1B fee and $4,500 L-1 fee to extensions for certain large employers.The proposal would particularly affect companies heavily dependent on foreign workers. About 71% of H-1B approvals in FY2025 were for continuing employment, and Indians accounted for nearly 78% of H-1B extensions.Meanwhile, the Department of Homeland Security is advancing a proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period that currently allows H-1B workers who lose their jobs to find another sponsor, change status or prepare to leave.The proposal is not yet law, but if implemented, losing a job would create a much tighter immigration deadline and increase workers' dependence on their sponsoring employer.Why the 60-day grace period changes are worrying is because of the labour market.“It’s a labor market affected by layoffs and AI-driven restructuring. An H-1B employee faces both the ordinary consequences of losing a job and an immigration consequence,” says K Edward Raleigh of Fragomen.“How difficult it is to find another sponsor within the available period depends heavily on the individual’s skills, seniority, industry and the willingness of prospective employers to undertake sponsorship,” he tells TOI, adding that employers continue to compete for exceptional talent, particularly in areas such as AI and machine learning.Also Read | Harsh reality for H-1B visa returnees: Changed Indian IT hiring landscape, lower salaries and fewer jobs But even as Boundless’ Xiao Wang acknowledges the vulnerability, he tells TOI that the labour market picture is more mixed than the layoff headlines.“The US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) unemployment rate for computer and mathematical occupations was 3.0% in August 2025, down from 3.4% a year earlier. USCIS approved 68,167 H-1B transfers in FY2025, and roughly 37% of H-1B workers who started at a new employer that year moved through the transfer route rather than through a new cap petition,” he explains.“We're hearing more mid-career Indian H-1B workers ask about self-petition options (O-1, EB-2 NIW, EB-1A) as insurance policies before they need them,” he says.According to Boundless’ CEO, for an Indian applicant, the deeper issue is the green card queue.“USCIS I-140 data puts India's EB-2 pending inventory at 351,142 petitions and EB-3 pending at 105,588. Cato Institute analysis by David Bier projects the EB-2 India wait for a new filing today at multiple decades under current visa issuance rates. Indian H-1B holders are therefore usually stuck on H-1B for many years, and losing a job during that window is a sharper cliff than for most other nationalities,” he cautions.Even as uncertainties mount, applications are still outpacing the allowed slots. Registrations still exceed slots by roughly five to one, says Xiao Wang. In the last posted H-1B registration cycle, USCIS had about 442,000 unique beneficiaries chasing 85,000 slots.Demand for the visa is not the constraint. What's changing is where the next generation of Indian technologists choose to build a career.Britta Glennon's Wharton research, cited in the NFAP report, finds that when US firms lose H-1B access they set up foreign affiliates and hire there at close to a one-for-one rate.“So global demand for the workers is not the constraint. Our read is that what has shifted is where the marginal Indian technologist bets, with Canada, the UK, Australia, and Germany picking up more of the flow,” Xiao Wang tells TOI.On the employer side, NFAP reports that the top seven India-based IT companies received 4,573 initial H-1B approvals in FY2025, a 37% drop from FY2024 and a 70% drop from FY2015. US tech companies now hold the top four employer slots for new H-1B approvals.So what do all these developments mean for Indian professionals? Experts are unanimous that caution is warranted and the environment continues to be volatile.Boundless Immigration CEO says that for Indian applicants, the H-1B is still a viable entry point, but applicants need to enter with realistic expectations.“H-1B is still a viable pathway if the applicant accepts that it may mean spending many years in temporary status rather than moving quickly to permanent residence,” Wang tells TOI. He shares some interesting data insights: The India numbers, from the USCIS I-140 report through Q2 FY2026For an early-career Indian engineer today, Canada may offer permanent residence far sooner than the US, he adds.Experts note that specialised skills continue to be in demand, and that would be the way forward as well.Akhil Chandna, Partner and Global People Solutions Leader, Grant Thornton Bharat believes that success in getting H-1B visas and retaining jobs in the US is likely to depend on a combination of specialised skills, career progression, employer sponsorship strategies and proactive immigration planning.“Professionals who remain aligned with high-demand sectors and invest in continuous upskilling are likely to be better positioned for long-term success,” he tells TOI.“Despite increased scrutiny, layoffs, and immigration uncertainty, the H-1B remains one of the most established routes for Indian professionals seeking a long-term career in the US. The US has however become less attractive for early-career professionals. Alternative countries such as Germany, the United Kingdom and Australia remain attractive,” he adds.“Professionals should focus on building differentiated skills, maintaining strong documentation of specialized expertise and evaluating immigration options with broader career goals. Early planning can help manage uncertainty and improve resilience across career transitions,” he recommends.K Edward Raleigh at Fragomen sums it up: The H-1B environment has undoubtedly become more complex and less forgiving in recent years. We are seeing a greater emphasis on immigration compliance and vetting, along with structural changes to the H-1B program.According to Raleigh, for Indian professionals looking at the US over the longer term, the distinction between temporary H-1B status and permanent residence is important.The H-1B can provide a durable means of working in the US, including in certain circumstances through extensions beyond the normal six-year limit while a Green Card case is pending. At the same time, India-born professionals face significant employment-based Green Card backlogs, which can create considerable uncertainty around the timing of permanent residence.“Those realities make long-term immigration planning increasingly important for both employees and employers,” he says.
Article Summary: H-1B visas have long been the main road for Indian professionals seeking employment, long-term career opportunities, and eventually even the green card in the US. But over the past two years, several changes in the application and selection criterion have added a huge layer of uncertainty. Indians still don’t make up the biggest chunk of individuals being granted the H-B visas.

Article Title: India, Japan deepen defence ties with maritime security pact; China challenge looms over Indo-Pacific
Article Text:
New Delhi, Aug 20 (ANI): Japan's Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi inspects the tri-services Guard of Honour at Manekshaw Centre, in New Delhi on Thursday. (ANI Photo/Naveen Sharma)

Rajnath Singh Announces Rs 8.75 Lakh Crore Defence Modernisation Push on 80th Independence Day

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and his Japanese counterpart Shinjirō Koizumi held a bilateral dialogue in New Delhi. Koizumi is on his maiden visit to India and the visit is seen as an expansion of the 'Special Strategic and Global Partnership' between the two countries, which is gaining importance in light of an assertive China across the Indo-Pacific region. The special strategic partnership, which was formalised in 2014 has continuously been strengthened by the leadership of the two countries, with PM Modi visiting Japan eight times. The strategic relationship has been anchored by shared democratic values and a common vision for a free and open Indo‑Pacific. During the meeting the defence minister of both the nations signed a Memorandum of Arrangement (MoA) on maritime security cooperation. This agreement provides a framework for strengthening cooperation between the naval forces of the two countries information sharing in the realm of maritime domain awareness and Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR).Defence cooperation between New Delhi and Tokyo has accelerated in recent years. A series of agreements since 2014 have institutionalised exchanges, ranging from the Memorandum of Defence Cooperation to the Reciprocal Provision of Supplies and Services pact signed in 2020.This framework has been operationalised during naval wargames such as MILAN and JAIMEX. These exercises have enabled seamless logistics during visit of ships and aircraft alike. The co‑development of Japan's UNICORN integrated communications antenna system for the Indian Navy, a deal that was formalised in 2024, represents the first joint equipment project between the two countries.The current visit has seen the defence ministers of both nations reaffirm their commitment to maritime security cooperation, mine countermeasures and joint shipbuilding. Japan’s technological expertise and India’s production capabilities are being aligned under the “Make in India” framework, with discussions on reciprocal ship repair facilities progressing. The two sides welcomed the expansion of bilateral exercises, including Dharma Guardian and JAIMEX, and looked ahead to Veer Guardian 26, which will see Japanese fighter aircraft participate in India for the first time. Both ministers also emphasised the importance of deepening defence R&D cooperation between Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Japan’s Acquisition Technology and Logistics Agency (ATLA), and confirmed plans to convene a Defence Industry Forum.The two countries have also decided to accelerate discussions towards convening the Fourth Japan-India foreign and defence ministerial (2+2) meeting that is scheduled to be held in Tokyo later this year. Besides this, Singh and Koizumi are working to further promote cooperation through the Indo-Pacific Logistics Network (IPLN). This initiative supports partner countries during natural disasters by facilitating the transportation of personnel and supplies for humaitarian assistance and disaster relief operations.Beyond defence, the visit reaffirmed the salience of economic security as a foundational pillar of the partnership. The synergy between Japan’s Free and Open Indo‑Pacific vision and India’s Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions (MAHASAGAR) initiative provides strategic impetus to cooperation. Both sides are committed to elevating economic security ties, recognising that prosperity and security are intertwined.The Japanese Defence Minister’s presence in India is thus more than ceremonial. It reflects a partnership that has evolved from cultural affinity into strategic convergence. The two nations have an enduring and rich cultural history, with links dating back to 752 AD, when Bodhisena, an Indian monk, consecrated the Great Buddha at Nara’s Todaiji Temple. In modern times, figures such as Swami Vivekananda, Rabindranath Tagore, Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose and Rash Behari Bose deepened the bonds of friendship. The Japan‑India Association, founded in 1903, is Japan’s oldest international friendship body. From Bodhisena’s consecration at Nara to joint naval drills in the Indian Ocean, the arc of India‑Japan relations is long, resilient and central pillar to keeping the Indo-Pacific open for all.
Article Summary: Shinjirō Koizumi is on his maiden visit to India and the visit is seen as an expansion of the 'Special Strategic and Global Partnership' between the two countries. The special strategic partnership, which was formalised in 2014, has continuously been strengthened by the leadership of both countries.

Article Title: Chandigarh was built as a planned city. So why does it keep sinking in the rain?
Article Text:
Chandigarh's planned infrastructure faces recurring monsoon flooding issues

72.4mm and the city starts to sink

72.4 mm of rain brought Chandigarh's drainage system to a standstill

When roads in Chandigarh are no longer roads

Two-wheelers struggle amid severe waterlogging

A road literally washed away

A footpath caved

City’s drainage problem predates Tuesday rain

Reasons for Chandigarh getting flooded

It is not just a case of ‘too much rain’

Floodwaters entered shops

Planned city, unplanned outcome?

City was planned but the outcome is unplanned

Poll Vote & Share your view Should the Municipal Corporation invest more in upgrading the city drainage infrastructure? Definitely yes No, focus on maintenance instead 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Bridge damaged after heavy rain





CHANDIGARH: Chandigarh was designed to be different — a city of sectors, wide roads, planned green spaces and carefully engineered infrastructure.Yet, every monsoon, the same question returns: how can a city built around such meticulous planning repeatedly turn into a maze of flooded roads, stranded vehicles and submerged markets? Tuesday’s deluge offered another uncomfortable answer.A mere two hours of intense rain was enough to expose how vulnerable parts of the city have become.The city got 72.4mm of rain in just two hours, the heaviest two-hour downpour of the current monsoon season.What followed was something familiar but harder to ignore as an occasional monsoon quirk: roads turned into rivers, cars were stranded in waist-high water, houses and shops were flooded and thousands of commuters were stuck in traffic jams.The worst affected stretches were not in one corner of Chandigarh. Rapid water accumulation was reported in Sectors 17, 22, 24, 36, 37, 42 and 43, as well as along Jan Marg, Madhya Marg, Industrial Area Phases I and II, Hallomajra and areas around the Old Secretariat.Water seeped into corridors and basements of Sector 22, one of the busiest commercial centers of the city, flooded parking areas and shopkeepers had to resort to flex boards, mops and rags to keep water out.More troubling was the state of the city’s traffic network. Vehicles crawled through submerged stretches, bumper-to-bumper, two-wheelers struggled to negotiate potholes and hidden manholes and many cars broke down while trying to cross flooded junctions.Ambulances heading to PGIMER were reportedly stranded on Madhya Marg, showing how quickly a waterlogging problem can turn into an emergency-services crisis.Residents also complained about the poor management of traffic when it was most needed. Police personnel were said to be scarce on parts of Madhya Marg, including the stretch between Transport Light Point and the IAF Museum light point.Some places saw barricades coming up but commuters said there was little on-ground help to divert traffic or guide motorists through alternate routes. In a city where traffic was normally orderly, the lack of visible intervention became a problem in itself.The rain didn’t just flood roads, it wrecked one. A portion of the carriageway on Madhya Marg between Transport Light Point and Grain Market Chowk reportedly caved in or washed away, forcing the traffic police to divert traffic coming from Panchkula through the road behind Police Lines toward ITI Light Point.The incident pointed to another vulnerability, that of road infrastructure itself becoming the next victim if drainage systems fail.Downed trees and limbs also added to the disruption. Trees or branches had fallen on the roads in several places, including Sector 22, making the already congested carriageways narrower and posing additional hazards.It was not just that motorists would be late getting home. Residents said a badly clogged or blocked road can delay ambulances, fire trucks and other emergency vehicles when every second counts.Thus, the problem of Chandigarh is not that it rained. The problem is that known amounts of rain still result in predictable failures in known places.The Municipal Corporation undertakes cleaning and desilting of road gullies and storm water drains before the monsoon every year. But several waterlogging hotspots keep flooding.This means that cleaning alone cannot compensate for an aging or inadequate drainage network.The figures offer us a useful context. According to Central Ground Water Board data, Chandigarh receives an annual average rainfall of about 1,009.8mm, of which about 844.9mm falls during the monsoon.So, the city’s drainage infrastructure has to cope with serious seasonal rainfall, not freak events, as a basic design parameter.Another irony. In fact, Chandigarh had a rainfall deficit earlier in the monsoon. The city received 240.2mm till July 25, against the normal of 359.6mm for June-July, a deficit of around 33%.July itself had 200.9mm against a normal of 204mm. The lesson is a good one: a city doesn’t need a season’s worth of excess rain to flood. And a short furious spell can swamp the system if rain falls faster than the water can drain away.But the problem is no longer confined to Chandigarh. Residents across Mohali, Zirakpur, Kharar and Nayagaon were in the same familiar cycle on Tuesday.In Mohali’s Sector 70 and Phase 11, school buses, cars, two-wheelers and pedestrians were seen passing through stagnant water on waterlogged streets.Not only were flooded roads an inconvenience for children and elderly residents, they also increased the risk of slips and falls and exposure to unhygienic stagnant water.This is where the larger conversation on Chandigarh’s monsoon problem is needed. The city was planned, zoned and built with infrastructure in mind.But a city planned with infrastructure for an earlier era may become vulnerable when asked to cope with today’s rainfall intensity, traffic volumes, construction patterns and expanding urbanization. The thing is not that the drains were cleaned before the monsoon.The question that has become is whether the entire storm-water system still holds up for the city of Chandigarh.So the flooding on Tuesday should not end with water being pumped out, fallen trees cleared and the damaged carriageway repaired.These are essential emergency responses, but they are not a flood management strategy. The real test is whether the administration can identify all recurring hotspots, map drainage capacity against rainfall intensity, clear bottlenecks and redesign vulnerable stretches before the next cloudburst does the audit for it.Because the problem with Chandigarh is not that it has never been planned. It’s that the city has changed faster than some of the infrastructure under it.If 72.4mm of rain in two hours can bring Sector 17, Sector 22, Madhya Marg and several peripheral areas to a halt, the question for policymakers is not when will it rain again.How many more monsoons will it take for Chandigarh’s drainage system to catch up to the city it was meant to serve?
Article Summary: 72.4 mm of rain brought Chandigarh's drainage system to a standstill. The city got 72.4mm of rain in just two hours, the heaviest two-hour downpour of the current monsoon season. Roads turned into rivers, cars were stranded in waist- high water, houses and shops were flooded.

Article Title: Who is Gautam Rangarajan? Indian-origin strategist appointed to key role by UK PM Andy Burnham
Article Text:
Indian-origin strategist Gautam Rangarajan.

Who is Gautam Rangarajan ?

What will Gautam Rangarajan do at No. 10?

Burnham's government overhaul

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has appointed Indian-origin strategist and former BBC executive Gautam Rangarajan as an Expert Adviser on Structure and Process in a newly created role at 10 Downing Street.Rangarajan, who brings decades of experience in strategy, organisational transformation and media, is set to take up the position this week.Rangarajan is a senior strategist and media executive with more than two decades of experience across media, creative industries and public service broadcasting.Before his new government role, he spent more than 30 years at the BBC, beginning his career as a radio music producer and eventually rising to become the broadcaster's Group Director for Strategy and Performance.His experience includes developing strategy in rapidly changing markets, leading large-scale transformation initiatives and handling complex policy and financial negotiations.The exact details of Rangarajan's responsibilities are yet to be outlined. However, the UK PM's office said his appointment draws on his experience in corporate strategy and transformation.His role comes as Burnham undertakes a broader restructuring of the machinery of government, including the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.Rangarajan is expected to play a role in the planned transformation at the heart of the British government.Away from strategy and public service, Rangarajan also has a creative side. He describes himself as a professional choral singer and music producer, alongside his work in corporate strategy and organisational transformation.The appointment comes as Burnham reshapes his government following his recent rise to the role of Labour Party leader and Prime Minister.His administration has announced structural changes, including the launch of No. 10 North in Manchester and the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.While the full scope of Rangarajan's new role remains unclear, his appointment places the former BBC executive at the centre of the UK government's planned transformation.
Article Summary: Gautam Rangarajan is a senior strategist and media executive. He has more than two decades of experience across media, creative industries and public service broadcasting. His appointment places the former BBC executive at the centre of the UK government's planned transformation.

Article Title: In 2020, Minnesota funded a $1.918 million Shell Rock River habitat program; by 2025, it had protected or restored 588 acres
Article Text:
Shell Rock River Watershed District (Image Credit: www.shellrock.org)

A habitat program takes shape

Three properties protected

Wetlands and prairie restored

More acres than planned

A longer-term conservation effort

In 2020, Minnesota approved $1.918 million for the Shell Rock River Watershed Habitat Restoration Program - Phase IX. According to a 2025 final report from the Lessard-Sams Outdoor Heritage Council, the program ultimately protected, restored or enhanced 588 acres of habitat in the Shell Rock River watershed, exceeding its original goal of 483 acres.The funding was provided under Minnesota Laws 2020, with the appropriation directed to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources for an agreement with the Shell Rock River Watershed District. The funding was intended to support land acquisition as well as the restoration and enhancement of aquatic habitat within the watershed. The program focused on several types of conservation work, including acquiring properties, restoring wetlands and improving aquatic habitat. The projects were selected using conservation planning and monitoring intended to identify areas where habitat improvements could provide significant benefits.The Shell Rock River Watershed is a shallow-lake system that supports fish, waterfowl and other wildlife. According to the final report, restoration projects were targeted at addressing habitat degradation and improving conditions for native fish, waterfowl and wildlife.One part of Phase IX involved acquiring three properties: the Glenville Property, the Bancroft Property, and the Church Lake Property. The District closed on the Glenville Property in March 2021 and the Bancroft Property in September 2021. For the Church Lake Property, the District transferred the deed to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources in December 2024 after acquiring and restoring the parcel.The final report says these acquisitions contributed to the program's permanent protection of 218 acres. Another 370 acres of habitat and wetlands were enhanced or restored through the program. Together, those accomplishments contributed to the reported total of 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored.The program included several restoration projects beyond property acquisition. The Bancroft Wetland Restoration was initiated in 2020, with construction beginning in June 2024 and largely completed by the fall of that year. Additional seeding work was completed in spring 2025. Another project focused on Panicum Prairie, where habitat enhancement work was carried out across 300 acres. The project involved native prairie vegetation and was substantially completed in February 2025, with final work completed in May.The program also supported the Fountain Lake In-Lake Habitat Project. Work included additional rock reefs and rock boulder clusters intended to improve fish habitat. The report notes that Phase IX funds were used to expand the scope of this work after the District determined additional funds were available. These projects addressed different parts of the watershed's ecosystem, from wetlands and prairie habitat to aquatic areas. The broader aim was to improve habitat conditions while protecting areas that could provide long-term benefits for wildlife.The program's original accomplishment plan called for 483 acres. By the end of the project, the final total had reached 588 acres, 105 acres more than initially planned. The report attributes the increase to the addition of the In-Lake Habitat Project and the Church Lake Property to Phase IX.According to the report, all grant funds were spent. The final grant expenditure remained $1.918 million, while the program's final total including leverage was $1.9479 million.The work is intended to continue beyond the end of the grant. The Shell Rock River Watershed District relies on multiple funding sources, including a local option sales tax, local levy and public funding, to maintain conservation projects. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources will also maintain the Church Lake Property, which it owns.The program's results illustrate how a single state-funded conservation effort can combine land protection, wetland restoration, prairie enhancement and aquatic habitat improvements. Rather than focusing on one habitat type, Phase IX combined several projects across the Shell Rock River watershed. By 2025, the program had moved beyond its original target, with the final report recording 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored. The completed work represents a combination of permanent land protection and habitat improvements designed to support Minnesota's fish, waterfowl and wildlife over the long term.
Article Summary: In 2020, Minnesota approved $1.918 million for the Shell Rock River Watershed Habitat Restoration Program - Phase IX. By 2025, the program had moved beyond its original target, with the final report recording 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored.

Article Title: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar to employees: Stop worrying about Anthropic; there is a chance they pull off the cover from ...
Article Text:
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar characterised the IPO not as an end point but as another step

Addressing the Anthropic question directly

OpenAI’s financial performance

Turnover in the executive ranks

OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar has told the employees during a recent all-hands meeting that the ChatGPT-maker “will be a public company in 2027,” though the debut could come sooner if business momentum continues, as reported by CNBC. “The IPO is not a finish line, it is a milestone, another fundraise,” she said, noting that OpenAI raised $122 billion in March, giving it flexibility. Friar addressed concerns about competitor Anthropic, which has also confidentially filed for an IPO. She told employees not to worry if Anthropic goes public first. “There is a chance they pull the cover off that confidential file in the coming weeks and become public in September. That’s OK, we are running our own race,” she said, according to sources.Friar characterized the IPO not as an end point but as another step in the company's fundraising journey, telling employees, according to the sources, that the IPO is not a finish line, it is a milestone. She pointed to the $122 billion OpenAI raised in March as a source of continued flexibility for the company going forward.OpenAI confidentially filed its IPO prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June but has not publicly disclosed a specific debut date.Its chief rival, Anthropic, has also confidentially filed its own prospectus with regulators and has reportedly been holding early meetings to gauge interest from potential investors.Friar used part of the meeting to get ahead of employee concerns that Anthropic might beat OpenAI to the public markets. She told staff that both companies are currently under confidential filing, and that there's a real chance Anthropic could make its filing public in the coming weeks and complete its debut as early as September. According to the sources, Friar told employees that would be fine, since OpenAI is focused on running its own race rather than measuring itself against Anthropic's timeline.OpenAI is under pressure to justify its $852 billion valuation ahead of a public listing, with investors pushing for more visibility into the company's financials. During the all-hands meeting, Friar shared slides showing that OpenAI's revenue run rate is up 35% quarter to date, its enterprise revenue run rate is up 50% quarter to date, and that its AI coding and work product tools have reached 20 million weekly active users.Separately, OpenAI told investors it generated $6.7 billion in revenue in the second quarter, up 18% from the first quarter, according to a Wall Street Journal report published later Wednesday. The company's annualized revenue run rate has recently topped $40 billion.Anthropic, meanwhile, told its own investors over the weekend that its annualized revenue run rate reached $65 billion by the end of July, a sevenfold increase from a year earlier, alongside a preliminary second-quarter revenue figure of $11.5 billion.Friar's remarks come after a stretch of executive departures at OpenAI that have reportedly left some of the company's financial backers uneasy about potential instability at the top. Revenue chief Denise Dresser left her role last week after just eight months at the company, two days after longtime executive Brad Lightcap announced he was ending an eight-year run at OpenAI to pursue a new venture. In July, product and business chief Fidji Simo stepped down from her role to focus on recovering from a chronic illness.With that turnover in the background, remaining leaders, including Friar, CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman, now face the task of projecting stability to investors already navigating concerns about rising competition, the growing adoption of cheaper open-weight AI models, and the volatile stock performance of SpaceX in its first two months as a public company.
Article Summary: OpenAI confidentially filed its IPO prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June but has not publicly disclosed a specific debut date. CFO Sarah Friar told employees not to worry if Anthropic goes public first. She told staff that both companies are currently under confidential filing, and that there's a real chance Anthropic could make its filing public in the coming weeks.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences







In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. The sale was based on economic and political reasons. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: MPD silent on 351 ‘mixed-use’ roads
Article Text:
New Delhi:





Master Plan for Delhi 2047 remains silent on 351 roads awaiting notification as mixed-use and commercial streets, leaving traders worried.A proposal was passed and forwarded to Delhi govt by MCD in 2007, but the clearance and notification remain pending. Under MPD 2047, mixed-use and commercial streets already notified by Delhi govt will continue with permitted activities. However, no such new road will be notified.The plan also permits mixed-use development along roads with a right of way of 30 metres or more, allowing commercial activities on the ground or first lower floor in buildings with stilt parking.Under MPD 2021, 2,538 roads and streets were notified for mixed-use and commercial activities. In 2018, amid political pressure and a sealing drive, Delhi govt submitted a draft notification to lieutenant governor. However, the final notification remains pending amid court and statutory oversight.D Thara, secretary of the capital development department under MoHUA, said a holistic approach would be adopted to address the notification issue. “The minister has given us two months Since the issue was before the high court and Supreme Court-appointed committee and MCD later identified additional streets, we need to take all these aspects into consideration.”Several commercial establishments have since come up along these roads, where traders are worried about sealing because the roads have not been formally declared permissible for mixed-land use. “Govt must clarify the statusof these roads and when they will be notified,” said Nitin Gupta, president of Kamla Nagar Traders Association.Rajendra Kapoor, senior vice-president of Delhi Vyapar Mahasangh, said the omission of any clear provision for regularising these roads in MPD 2047 had worried traders. He said the long-pending issue should not be left ambiguous in Delhi’s future planning framework.
Article Summary: Master Plan for Delhi 2047 remains silent on 351 roads awaiting notification as mixed-use and commercial streets. A proposal was passed and forwarded to Delhi govt by MCD in 2007, but the clearance and notification remain pending. Traders are worried about sealing because the roads have not been declared permissible for mixed-land use.

Article Title: Hindu College staff association passes no-confidence motion against principal over ‘admission irregularities’
Article Text:
New Delhi:

TOI





Hindu College Staff Association has passed a “no-confidence motion” against principal Anju Srivastava over alleged irregularities in admissions under the sports and ECA quotas, alleging that extra admissions were made in some programmes despite the issue having been flagged by the college.Under Delhi University rules, sports and ECA admissions can together account for up to 5% of a college’s total strength. In Hindu College’s case, this worked out to 48 seats — 33 under sports and 15 under ECA. The rules further provide that a programme can get a maximum of 20% of the seats under the quota. This meant a programme could get up to seven sports and three ECA seats. However, commerce received 11 sports and six ECA seats, taking its total to 17 — seven more than the prescribed limit. Political science received nine sports and six ECA seats, taking its total to 15 — five more than the limit.The issue was flagged by the college’s ECA and sports committees in the staff council, following which the principal wrote to DU’s dean of admissions on Aug 11 seeking clarification on the allocations made through the university’s centralised admission system. She asked DU to “verify the allocation and get the same rectified at the earliest”.In its Aug 14 response, DU’s dean of admissions acknowledged that there had been an error in the allocation. It said the 20% cap was “inadvertently applied at the programme level rather than separately to the sports/ECA quota”, which led to some programmes getting more seats than the prescribed limit.DU Registrar Vikas Gupta said the issue was not limited to Hindu College and had occurred in several other colleges as well. “While allocating seats, we apply several formulas. In the ECA and sports allocation, a third formula was missed. But even after that, the overall 5% rule has not been violated and the merit has not been compromised. We could not cancel the extra allocations because the first round had already concluded. The necessary corrections will therefore be made in the subsequent rounds. ,” he said.Responding to, principal Srivastava said, “The merit has not been falsified. The allocation is done by the university and the college has no role in it. The university has clearly communicated that there was an inadvertent error in the allocation in this round, and they will ensure there are no such errors in the subsequent rounds.”Staff council secretary Chandrachur Singh , however, alleged that the issue was not an isolated incident. “There have been various incidents in the past where the principal has turned administration into an autocratic working,” .The association, on Aug 18, passed a resolution expressing “dismay at the role of the principal”. It has sought an impartial inquiry into the alleged rule violations and possible corrupt practices.AISA, NSUI, KYS and other students also protested on campus against the administration Thursday.
Article Summary: Hindu College Staff Association has passed a “no-confidence motion’ against principal Anju Srivastava. The issue was flagged by the college’s ECA and sports committees in the staff council. The principal wrote to DU’S dean of admissions on Aug 11 seeking clarification on the allocations.

Article Title: Loose edible oil sale banned as Maharashtra FDA tightens supply rules
Article Text:
The FDA has mandated statewide compliance for the edible oil industry, banning loose sales.





MUMBAI: FDA on Thursday issued a statewide 14-clause compliance and enforcement order for the edible oil industry, binding the entire supply chain—from manufacturers and distributors to retailers, online sellers and the labelling industry.The order mandates sale only in “sealed, tamper-evident and fully labelled packages”, prohibiting loose or unpackaged oil. Manufacturers or distributors dispatching oil in loose form will be treated as primary violators.The action follows inspections that found unlicensed businesses, substandard oil exceeding acid value and trans-fat limits, adulteration with cheaper oils, unauthorised mustard oil blending, relabelling to conceal sources and dates, and repackaging of near-expiry oil.FDA commissioner Tukaram Mundhe said the order covers expeller and solvent extraction units, refiners, manufacturers of vanaspati, vegetable fats, bakery shortening, margarine and table spreads, besides importers and transporters.Maharashtra has 497 edible oil manufacturers—212 centrally licensed and 285 state licensed. Of 1,247 samples tested over the past year, 1,142 met standards, while 77 were substandard, 13 unsafe and 15 misbranded.Mundhe warned that malpractices disproportionately affect consumers buying oil in small quantities, citing risks from contamination and oxidative compounds in repeatedly heated oil.“The worst impact of malpractice in this sector is borne by ordinary consumers who purchase oil in small quantities. Argemone contamination has previously caused epidemic dropsy outbreaks resulting in heart failure, glaucoma and death. Lead leaches into oil from rusted and spot-welded cans, acting as a cumulative toxin that impairs brain development in children,” Mundhe said.“Trans-fatty acids and oxidative compounds formed in repeatedly heated oil are linked to atherosclerosis, hypertension, liver and kidney damage, stroke and an elevated risk of cancer.”
Article Summary: FDA issued a statewide 14-clause compliance and enforcement order for the edible oil industry. Order mandates sale only in “sealed, tamper-evident and fully labelled packages’ Action follows inspections that found unlicensed businesses, substandard oil exceeding acid value.

Article Title: 40 passengers from Dubai stranded as connecting SpiceJet flights cancelled
Article Text:
The passengers said they received no prior information from the airline





Mumbai: SpiceJet’s operational troubles spilt over into passenger chaos at Mumbai airport, with more than 40 passengers stranded overnight after connecting flights to Darbhanga and Gorakhpur were cancelled. The passengers, who had arrived from Dubai early Thursday, said they received no intimation and were left without food or accommodation. Airport police eventually stepped in and arranged their stay.The incident comes as SpiceJet continues to grapple with mounting operational pressures, with its July cancellation rate touching 8.58% and the airline facing an NCLT matter over insolvency proceedings. SpiceJet escaped immediate insolvency on Wednesday after lessor Aviator ML withdrew its Rs 60-crore insolvency plea following a settlement. But seven other lessor petitions remain, keeping the insolvency threat alive.Sources said airport police held a meeting at 11am on Thursday with SpiceJet, CISF , DGCA, BCAS and Mumbai Airport International Airport Ltd (MAIL) officials. Police warned the airline that a repeat of such an incident could lead to an FIR under the BNS provision relating to criminal breach of trust.The stranded passengers said many had rushed home from the Gulf for family emergencies. Some were travelling to attend funerals, while another passenger said his wife was in an ICU in Gorakhpur.“There was no message or communication from SpiceJet when we took the flight from Dubai on Wednesday about the cancellation in Mumbai. There were no arrangements made by the airline. We approached the airport police when airline staff told us that we could complain anywhere but nothing would happen. Police made a diary entry and arranged accommodation and food for more than 40 passengers at a dormitory near the airport,” said Prem Kumar, who works at a hotel in Dubai.Ethesam ul Haq said he had rushed from Dubai after his mother died on Wednesday. “I rushed from Dubai on Wednesday to attend my mother’s funeral at 10am on Thursday. Now I will reach on Friday, when everything will be over. I don’t have money to buy another ticket and have to depend on the rescheduled flight on Friday morning to Darbhanga.” MD Ansari from Gorakhpur too will be missing the funeral of his father-in-law on Wednesday.“My wife is in the ICU. I am stuck at the airport and worried about her condition. I paid Rs 16,400 for the ticket. After the chaos, the airline finally gave me a boarding pass for tomorrow’s flight,” said Gorakhpur resident Akbar Ali.Another passenger, Shamse Alam, said he and several others were returning to India after nearly two years. “We never received any intimation from the airline. If we had been informed 14 hours earlier, as the airline claims, we would have booked another flight. That claim is false,” he said.The airport police also handled a separate group of around 38 passengers from a SpiceJet flight from Goa to Mumbai. The flight was delayed by four hours and, after landing in Mumbai, the pilot reportedly reached his permissible duty limit. The passengers, who were to continue to Delhi, were left stranded.A SpiceJet spokesperson said: “The information regarding the passengers from Dubai is factually incorrect. The SpiceJet flight from Mumbai to Darbhanga on August 20 was cancelled due to operational reasons, and the cancellation was communicated to passengers 14 hours prior to the scheduled departure. The claim that passengers were denied a refund is also incorrect. Passengers were offered the option of either a full refund or rescheduling on the next available flight. SpiceJet communicates schedule changes to passengers through the registered contact details provided at the time of booking, in line with standard industry practice. Where a booking has been made through a travel agent and the agent’s contact details have been provided as the registered contact, the communication is sent to those details.”
Article Summary: More than 40 passengers stranded overnight after connecting flights to Darbhanga and Gorakhpur were cancelled. The passengers, who had arrived from Dubai early Thursday, said they received no intimation and were left without food or accommodation. Airport police eventually stepped in and arranged their stay.

Article Title: Veil-clad women posing as customers flee with 1.5kg gold from Sambhajinagar jewellery store
Article Text:
Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar

:





A gang of six, including four veil-clad women, allegedly stole a box containing around 1.5kg of gold ornaments from a jewellery shop in the busy Shahganj-City Chowk market area on Thursday after posing as customers. Considering the market value of gold on Thursday, the stolen items would be worth roughly Rs 2.25 crore.The theft sparked concern among traders in one of the city’s busiest commercial hubs.Police commissioner Pravin Pawar said the suspects did not enter the shop together. “Some of them arrived posing as customers. They were followed by their accomplices at different intervals, apparently to avoid suspicion and divert the attention of the staff,” he said.Investigators said the women engaged employees by asking to see various pieces of jewellery and pretending to make purchases, while the others allegedly monitored the shop. Taking advantage of the distraction, the gang allegedly fled with a box containing the gold items.The police are probing whether the shop was specifically targeted after a recce or whether the gang seized an opportunity after spotting a vulnerable situation.The manner in which the suspects entered separately has strengthened suspicions of a pre-planned theft.Teams have begun scrutinising CCTV footage from the jewellery shop and surrounding areas to identify the accused and track their movements before and after the theft. Cameras installed across the Shahganj market area are also being examined to determine the escape route.The role of the two men accompanying the women is under investigation. The police are also trying to ascertain whether the gang used a vehicle and if its registration details can help trace the suspects.No arrests had been reported till late Thursday.
Article Summary: A gang of six, including four veil-clad women, allegedly stole a box containing around 1.5kg of gold ornaments from a jewellery shop in the busy Shahganj-City Chowk market area on Thursday. Considering the market value of gold on Thursday, the stolen items would be worth roughly Rs 2.25 crore.
